Equichordal

GeometryCurvesInvariants
What it shows: A shape with a centre O and a bar through it: turn the bar any way you like and its length stays the same.
How to play: Drag the blue or green end of the bar, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Change Power, Shift and Frequency, tick “Sine formula” to see the curve, and press Clear to start again.
Look for the math

Mary Krimmel asked whether the centre of a circle is the only point where every chord through it has the same length. The answer is no: there are many other curves. The live cut-the-knot article now shows a GeoGebra model; the Java applet embedded in the 2007 archive of the same page is the one this port follows.

A fixed length in both directions

An equichordal point O has the same chord length in every direction. If a boundary point in one direction is at distance r(t) from O, the one in the opposite direction is at r(t + π), so the chord is r(t) + r(t + π). Make that sum constant and O is equichordal. The applet's curve gives r(t) + r(t + π) = 2 × Scale × Shift, which is 184 board units here. The logic test checks this sum at 1.5 million samples and checks the dragged chord's length over the whole selector range. Two harmless quirks stay: at Shift = 1 the tiny floating-point error at π can make the opening chord read 185 instead of 184, and the 640-pixel slider snaps a chosen Shift of 2.0 to 1.99.

Why odd numbers work

In polar coordinates the applet uses r(t) = Scale × (Shift + sin(Frequency × t)Power). Since sin(k(t + π)) = (−1)k sin(kt), an odd Frequency and an odd Power make the sine term change sign after half a turn. The two terms cancel in the sum, leaving the constant 2 × Scale × Shift. Even values do not cancel: the logic test shows the sum then varies with t. That is the page's “why?” answered.

Many curves, but only one such point

The page's r(t) = 2 + sin(t) is one example; any f with f(t) + f(t + π) = const works, giving a four-parameter family when you start with a sine wave. Here Radius in the page's formula is the applet's Scale, which depends on Shift. Because r(t) ≥ 0, every point of these regions can be joined to O by a segment inside the region, so they are star-shaped; all convex regions are star-shaped. Rychlik proved that no star-shaped region can have two equichordal points, so a curve like this can have only one, even though there are infinitely many curves to choose from.

Try Frequency 3 and Power 3, tick Sine formula, then drag A around: watch B land at the far end of the same-length bar.
